passages.t: A town besieged, and a cruel treaty
passages.happening:
Nahash the Ammonite comes up and lays siege to Jabesh-gilead. The men of the town offer to surrender: “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you” (verse 1).

Nahash names his price. “I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel” (verse 2).

The elders ask for seven days to send messengers through Israel. ‘If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you’ (verse 3).

The messengers come to Gibeah, Saul's town, and when the people hear the news they all weep aloud (verse 4). ‘Just then Saul was returning from the field, behind his oxen’ (verse 5). He asks why the people are weeping, and they tell him.
passages.hearers:
The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan, with their capital at Rabbah, modern Amman. They fought Israel often, especially over Gilead, the hilly land east of the Jordan where the tribes of Gad and Reuben and half of Manasseh had settled. Jabesh-gilead lay in the north of Gilead.

The town had an old bond with Saul's tribe. At the end of the book of Judges, the surviving men of Benjamin took wives from Jabesh-gilead, so many Benjamites had family there.

A treaty, literally a covenant, was the normal way to end a siege. The weaker town surrendered and served the stronger. Nahash's condition was meant as public humiliation, a reproach on all Israel, and it may also have been meant to leave the men unable to fight. That he grants them seven days to look for help shows how sure he is that none will come. Israel without a united leader looked helpless.

The Dead Sea Scroll copy of Samuel called 4QSamuel-a has a paragraph before this chapter that is not in the standard Hebrew text. It tells how Nahash had been oppressing the tribes of Gad and Reuben in the same cruel way, and how some who escaped fled to Jabesh. Some modern translations print it, and others do not, judging that it may be a later addition. It would explain why Nahash was already at Jabesh.

The new king is still working his father's fields. That says something about how new and small Israel's kingship was.
passages.later: The bond between Jabesh-gilead and Benjamin goes back to the end of Judges, where the men of Benjamin took wives from the town (Judges 21:12).
passages.asks: The men of Jabesh asked for seven days to find someone to save them. Ask who near you is waiting for help that no one seems ready to bring. And ask whether you would weep at their news, as the people of Gibeah did, and then do nothing.

passages.t: The Spirit, and a rescue at dawn
passages.happening:
“When Saul heard their words, the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger” (verse 6).

He cuts a pair of oxen into pieces and sends them through all Israel with a warning: “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel” (verse 7). ‘Then the terror of the LORD fell upon the people, and they turned out as one man’ (verse 7). At Bezek he counts 300,000 men of Israel and 30,000 of Judah (verse 8).

The men of Jabesh are told that help will come ‘tomorrow by the time the sun is hot’ (verse 9). They tell Nahash that tomorrow they will come out to him (verse 10).

The next day Saul divides the army into three companies. During the morning watch they break into the Ammonite camp and strike them down until the heat of the day, and the survivors are scattered so that no two are left together (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The chapter reads like one of the rescue stories in Judges. An enemy oppresses, the people cry out, the Spirit of God rushes upon a leader, the leader gathers Israel, and the enemy is beaten. Saul comes in from the field behind his oxen, as Gideon was found threshing wheat. He hears the news, the Spirit comes, and his anger burns. The victory is presented as the Spirit's work through Saul, not only Saul's own courage.

Sending the pieces of oxen was a threat: whoever did not come would see his own oxen treated the same way. Saul uses the very animals he was driving. Readers of Judges would remember a grim parallel. After the crime at Gibeah, a summons sent in pieces through Israel led to civil war. Saul, from that same town, uses a summons like it to unite the tribes, not to divide them.

The terror of the LORD was an overwhelming awe sent by God. It moved the people to act together, as one man. God is at work in the people's answer as well as in Saul.

The numbers in verse 8 raise the same question as other large numbers in Samuel: whether the word for thousand means a count or a military unit.

The morning watch was the last of the three watches of the night, the hours just before dawn, a favorite time for surprise attacks.
passages.later:
Gideon was found working when God called him, ‘threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites’ (Judges 6:11).

The book of Judges ends with a summons sent through Israel in pieces, and the people's cry, “Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day” (Judges 19:30). That summons led to war among the tribes. Saul's leads to a rescue.
passages.asks: Saul's anger burned at cruelty done to people who could not defend themselves. Ask what cruelty in the world makes you angry, and what your anger moves you to do. And ask whether your anger serves the helpless or only yourself.

passages.t: Mercy to his critics, and the kingship renewed
passages.happening:
After the victory the people say to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!” (verse 12).

Saul will not allow it: “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel” (verse 13).

Samuel says, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there” (verse 14). So all the people go to Gilgal and confirm Saul as king before the LORD. They offer peace offerings, ‘and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is Saul's finest moment. The men who had despised him in chapter 10 are in danger, and he spares them. He gives the credit for the victory to the LORD. Kingship is at its best here: a leader who serves the people, rescues the oppressed, shows mercy to his critics, and gives God the glory.

The word for salvation here means rescue from an enemy. In the Old Testament it is always finally God's work, even when a human leader is the instrument.

Samuel calls the people to renew the kingship. Scholars debate what that means: restoring something disputed after the grumbling of 10:27, confirming Saul in public after his first victory, or renewing the covenant. Either way, the kingship is now established with the people's full support.

The people of Jabesh will not forget this day. When Saul dies on Mount Gilboa, they will travel all night to recover his body and bury it (31:11-13). Anyone who knows how Saul's story ends will feel the weight of this bright beginning.
passages.later:
Years later David thanked the men of Jabesh-gilead for their loyalty, ‘because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord when you buried him’ (2 Samuel 2:5).

A proverb gives the reason not to take revenge into one's own hands: ‘Wait on the LORD, and He will save you’ (Proverbs 20:22).
passages.hard:
Why does Saul seem to become king three times, in chapters 10 and 11?

Saul is anointed in private (10:1), chosen by lot at Mizpah (10:17-24), and then made king by the people at Gilgal (11:15). That can look like three different accounts of how he came to the throne.

Many critical scholars see here several traditions about Saul's rise, some warmer toward kingship than others, gathered by the book's editors. Others read the steps as one process that fits how leaders were recognized in the ancient world: chosen by God in private through a prophet, chosen in public before the tribes, and confirmed after proving himself in battle. Samuel himself calls the Gilgal event a renewal, which supports the idea of a process in stages.

Readers on both sides agree that the finished account presents Saul's kingship as coming from God, confirmed by the people, and proven in action.
passages.asks: Saul refused to kill the men who had despised him. Ask whom you would like to see put in their place now that you have been proved right. And ask what it would look like to say, as Saul did, that the day belongs to the LORD.
